name: Hyacinth Blue
lede: Hyacinth blue is a deep purplish blue named for the flower, and its older echo, the biblical hyacinth blue, was a shade of cloth that stood beside scarlet and purple.

sections.title: Flower and cloth
sections.body:
Paterson gives hyacinth blue as a purplish blue that was popular in the 1930s, and the related word hyacinthine as the purplish blue of the hyacinth, which he also stretches to violet or pink [1]. The family has a red member too: hyacinth red is a reddish orange [1].

The older use is in cloth. Gage recounts a tale in which maidens picked to make the Temple's veil divide the work by lot, one spinning gold, another cotton or linen, and others hyacinth-blue, scarlet and purple [2]. In that line-up the blue is one dye among the costly ones, not a flower color. Which blue the old texts meant is not settled by the books we read.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
This swatch comes from the charts: it carries over from Ridgway's 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors*, reappears on plate X of his 1912 atlas, and in ISCC-NBS block 197 is called a moderate purplish blue, 3.3 units away [3]. Maerz and Paul date two nearby plates to 1388 and 1912 [3]. It is a deeper, more violet color than Paterson's 1930s blue, so treat his date as the word's fashion and the swatch as the chart's choice [1][3].

The nearest named color is [[indigo]], 9.7 units away, and Roslyn Blue is a near-duplicate, 2.4 apart [3]. Where [[blue]] pulls toward [[violet]] and [[purple]], this is where they meet.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Hyacinth blue is very rare in paint: 10 of 23,781 paintings in our archive (0.04 per cent), 5 by the stricter within-painting lens, rarer than 75 per cent of named colors [4]. With so few cases we draw no trend from them.

The earliest match is a work of 1500 by Maestro de la Sisla, a look-alike hue 386 years before the name's first record in our sources, 1886; the third-earliest is already 1903 [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test. [4]

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 212

True or false: hyacinth blue is a common color in museum paintings.

openers: Hyacinth red exists too, and it is a reddish orange, not a red-violet.
Hyacinth blue is rarer in paintings than 75 per cent of named colors: when you see it, take note.
